catalog_quote: [Harley & Leyva 2009:236] Hiaki words have a lexical high tone or pitch accent on a particular syllable. The default placement of this tone is on the leftmost syllable of the word, but certain lexically marked words bear tone on a later syllable. This tone placement may be contrastive, as in, for example, ánia 'to help' and anía 'world'. ... [fn. 5] both pitch and stress play a role in the prominence of a Hiaki syllable ... [Haugen 2003:76] Yaqui marks prominence through pitch accent, or high tone. This occurs on the first or second mora of the word, in isolated words (Demers, Escalante and Jelinek 1999). ... Those words which have initial moras without high tone have initial moras that are lexically extrametrical—and thus the tone is assigned to the first available mora (i.e. the second mora of the word). Syllable weight is not a factor in assigning high tone, and high tone assignment …

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check passes: every quoted sentence is verbatim at the cited page in the held text layers (Harley & Leyva 2009:236 + fn.5; Haugen 2003:76-77; Crumrine 1961 sect.4, now also in the full Open Arizona copy at p.5). (2) The deciding sources are a peer-reviewed IJAL article by the language's principal documentary linguist and a working paper, both describing prosody as background to reduplication and relaying Demers, Escalante & Jelinek 1999; the dedicated study (Demers et al. 1999, paywalled) and the reference grammar (Dedrick & Casad 1999, print only) are not held, so the record is second-hand for its key facts -- hence 'adequate' rather than 'well-sourced'. (3) Four open items fetched sources now (Martínez Fabián & Munguía Duarte 2006 instrumental; Hafner 2018 instrumental with page-cited summaries of Demers et al. and Dedrick & Casad; Hiaki pedagogical grammar 2017 Lesson 30; Crumrine 1

sources.citation: Hafner, Florian. 2018. Acoustic and perceptual correlates of the Hiaki pitch accent. University of Arizona, Department of Linguistics (COMPSS18v3, posted at arizonahiaki.org/analysis/pitch-accent). 76 pp.
sources.quote: p.4: 'Hiaki possesses a lexical pitch accent creating minimal pairs such as héeka wind and heéka drank. Demers et al. (1999, p. 41) state that such pairs are true minimal pairs ... the pitch accent is lexically specified'; p.5 'the lexical pitch accent attaches to morae. In káate ... first mora whereas ... second mora in kaáte'. p.15: 'Regarding the placement of the pitch accent, all the studies have highlighted that the pitch accent is likely to attach to either the first or the second syllable'; Dedrick & Casad 1999: two distinctive pitches, high pitch 'attaches to the first or second syllab
sources.locator: pp. 4-5 (sec 1.2.1), pp. 13-16 (review of Fabián & Duarte 2006, Hagberg 2008, Dedrick & Casad 1999:28-29, Demers et al. 1999:41-46), p. 14 fn. 6
sources.note: Most recent acoustic/perception study (one Arizona speaker, 36 listeners) with a page-cited review of Demers et al. 1999, Dedrick & Casad 1999, Hagberg 2008; confirms lexical mora-based pitch accent on 1st/2nd mora.

sources.citation: Sanchez, Jose, Alex Trueman, Maria Florez Leyva, Santos Leyva Alvarez, Mercedes Tubino Blanco, Hyun-Kyoung Jung, Louise St. Amour & Heidi Harley. 2017. Hiaki pedagogical grammar, Volume One (2017-06-26 final). University of Arizona Hiaki project, arizonahiaki.org. 217 pp.
sources.quote: 'Most words in Hiaki have a vowel that requires more emphasis. It is usually the first one. However, in some words the emphasis appears on the second vowel' with pairs ánia/anía, yó'oko/yoóko, bwíchia/bwichía, váchia/vachía, ká'ate/kaáte, wíuta/wiúta; 'it is important to memorize which words have accent on the second syllable'; 'in Hiaki, the pitch accented vowels are pronounced more with a higher pitch, but not so much additional loudness'.

sources.citation: Martínez Fabián, Constantino & Ana Lidia Munguía Duarte. 2006. Yaqui: a double aligned trochaic feet language. Paper, Friends of Uto-Aztecan Conference, 23-26 Aug 2006, Universidad de Sonora. 22 pp. (ms cited by Harley & Leyva 2009 fn.5)
sources.quote: p.2: Langendoen & Munguía 1996 'claim that lexical words always bear stress either on the first or second mora ... trochaic foot ... for those words with stress on the second mora, they assumed an underlying iambic foot'; Demers et al. 1999 'a high tone occurs either on the first or second syllable of a word'; minimal pairs káate/kaáte, yóoko/yoóko, téeka/teéka. p.1/21: acoustic data from two Sonora speakers -> 'Yaqui must be classified as a lexical stress-pitch language': unmarked pattern = double-aligned trochee [S W] stress with [L H] pitch; marked patterns single-aligned trochee [S W]/[H L
sources.note: Instrumental (F0/intensity/duration) study of two Sonora speakers; confirms lexical 1st/2nd placement and adds that stress and pitch prominence can sit on different syllables (unmarked S-W stress with L-H pitch) -- the realization caveat our notes already flag.

sources.citation: Crumrine, Lynne S. 1961. The Phonology of Arizona Yaqui, with Texts. Anthropological Papers of the University of Arizona 5. Tucson: University of Arizona Press. 46 pp. (full open-access copy, Open Arizona; previously held only as 3 Rosetta page images)
sources.quote: p.5: 'Most Yaqui words have stress accent ... each stem, compound, or idiom said in isolation is characterized by a relatively stable pattern of relative loudness of syllables, though there is perturbation of this stress in running discourse'; 4.1-4.3 stress-timed rhythm, in spans of 2-3-syllable words 'every other syllable is stressed'; 5.6 'tone and stress in running discourse are not to be confused'. No placement rule and no weight statement anywhere in the monograph.

sources.note: The standard reference grammar (Glottolog's top-ranked grammar); pp. 26-29 treat high/low pitch on the first or second syllable, pitch shift under affixation, and state that stress is not prominence-bearing except in a few closed-syllable words (per Hafner 2018:14 fn.6 and Harley & Leyva 2009 fn.5) -- directly relevant to our LEXICAL vs TONAL-OR-PITCH-ACCENT choice and to the weight question.
